title: He descended
hook: the creed says he went down to the dead; the Orthodox icon shows him pulling Adam and Eve out

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was atonement: ransom, sacrifice, love's example, victory. Your line was love went all the way.

Between Good Friday and Easter Sunday there's a day easy to skip: Saturday. The body is in the tomb. The disciples are hiding. Nothing seems to happen. Right there, between buried and rose again, the creed slips in a strange line. The old prayer book reads: "He descended into hell." Hell? Now look at the Easter icon of Orthodox churches. Christ in shining white, standing on two broken doors, crossed beneath his feet. Around him, scattered keys, snapped locks, loose nails. Below, a dark pit. With each hand he grabs someone by the wrist, an old man and an old woman, and hauls them out of their tombs. Adam and Eve. Today's word is that line in the creed.
screen: `THE SILENT SATURDAY.` → `HE DESCENDED INTO HELL.` → `BROKEN DOORS, AND TWO WRISTS.`

segments.voice: First, the word hell. The King James Bible uses it for the Greek Hades: in Acts, Peter says of Jesus that "his soul was not left in hell." Hades, like the Hebrew Sheol, is the realm of the dead, where all the dead were thought to go; that's most likely the creed's meaning, which is why some modern versions say he descended to the dead. So Jesus really died, all the way, as every human being does. The Bible hints at more. First Peter says he "went and preached unto the spirits in prison," and later that the gospel was preached "also to them that are dead." From those verses grew an old Christian story: on Holy Saturday, Christ went down to the dead and set free those who had waited for him, from Adam and Eve on. Medieval England called it the harrowing of hell, the raid on hell. An ancient Holy Saturday sermon, by an unknown writer, imagines Christ taking Adam's hand and saying, more or less: wake up, sleeper, I didn't make you to be held in hell. Christians read the line in different ways. Orthodox and Catholics generally see Christ freeing the righteous dead. Calvin read it as Christ suffering the full weight of separation from God on the cross. Some churches leave the line out. Under them all runs one hope: no place is so dark that God won't go there. A psalm already said it: "If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there."
screen: `HADES: THE REALM OF THE DEAD.` · `HE REALLY DIED.` · `THE HARROWING OF HELL.` · `NO PLACE TOO DARK.` · then, large: `IF I MAKE MY BED IN HELL, BEHOLD, THOU ART THERE.`

segments.voice: Let someone you've lost come to mind, and see their face; notice what you miss. If you pray, pray for them, as Catholic and Orthodox Christians do, or give thanks to God for them, as others prefer. If you don't, just hold them in mind, with love.
He descended. The creed's line that Christ went down to the dead, all the way, and, in the old story, brought them out.
Your line: even there. The hope Christians hold: no place is too dark for God. Day three hundred three.

howItsDone: Many churches keep Holy Saturday as a quiet day of waiting; Orthodox Christians sing of Christ trampling down death, and the Easter icon, the Anastasis, shows him lifting Adam and Eve from their tombs.

fork.setup: you're painting the Orthodox icon of Easter. you've painted Christ in white. what's he doing?
options: standing on broken doors, pulling Adam and Eve from their tombs.
sitting on a throne in heaven.
fork.reveal: the Anastasis icon shows Christ on the shattered gates of death, grasping Adam and Eve by the wrists and lifting them out.

original.note: Greek: Hades, the unseen realm of the dead. The word behind hell in this line of the creed.

trapdoor: what you thought: the creed says Jesus went to hell to be punished.
what it means: he truly died and went to the dead, and, many Christians say, set free those waiting there.
what a scholar hears: Hades and Sheol, 1 Peter 3:19 and 4:6, and a medieval English word, harrowing: a raid.

chat.says: Why does the creed say Jesus descended into hell? Wasn't he good?
options: There it means the realm of the dead: he truly died, and no place is too dark for God.
It means he was punished there forever for something he had done wrong.
It's a recent line no church ever said until the last hundred years.
chat.meaning: The creed's hell is Hades, the realm of the dead. Christ died all the way, and the old story says he brought the dead out.

Hades.meaning: Greek name for the realm of the dead

Sheol.meaning: Hebrew name for the realm of the dead

Holy Saturday.meaning: the quiet day between Good Friday and Easter

harrowing of hell.meaning: old English name for Christ's raid on the realm of the dead

notes: 'He descended into hell' as in BCP 1662; many modern ecumenical texts (e.g. ELLC) say 'he descended to the dead'.
The icon description (Anastasis) is standard; confirm details (crossed doors, keys, locks, nails).
Ancient Homily on Holy Saturday: paraphrased; author unknown (sometimes attributed to Epiphanius). Confirm paraphrase.
'Some churches leave the line out': e.g. some Methodist usage (Wesley's Sunday Service omitted it). Confirm.
Practice mentions praying for the dead (common in Catholic, Orthodox, some Anglican practice) and giving thanks (preferred by many Protestants), without ranking.

Softened 'All agree on one thing' to 'Across these readings runs one shared hope', and 'doesn't mean' to 'most likely doesn't mean' for the place of punishment, since some readers (e.g. Calvin) tie the line to bearing God's judgment.
